fixes.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says the married man's “…interests are divided.” Look at what sits on each side. The married man is concerned about “…the affairs of this world, how he can please his wife…” while the unmarried man is concerned about “…the work of the Lord…” I think that's the split Paul is pointing at: two sets of concerns, both asking for the same man's attention.

A broken word never comes up in this verse, baker. The man's worry is that he's acting inappropriately toward his betrothed, and Paul answers, “…let him do as he wishes; he is not sinning; they should get married.” So the only verdict Paul gives is that he is not sinning. Nobody is hauling out a guilty verdict here.

Apollos, an eloquent Jew from Alexandria (Acts 18:24), isn't in this passage. Paul's last line is, “And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.” He doesn't line up anyone's approval to back up his judgment. What he points to is the Spirit of God, and he says it with an “I think.”
